newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O.Licht - World coffee production estimate.
newsitem.headline: F.O.Licht - World coffee production estimate.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician
F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to
Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

The ACPC technical group when it met recently in Costa Rica forecast world output of coffee in 1996/97 at 99 million bags while consumption was put at 100 million bags.

In our first forecast for the season we have come to the somewhat lower figure of 96.5 million bags. Though that is nearly 9 million bags up on the weather damaged 1995/96 crop it is still less than likely demand so producers' hopes for stable or even higher prices do not seem to be far fetched.

What must not be overlooked, however, is that production estimates are prone to large revisions due to a lack of transparency in some countries and also the inclination that has sometimes been noticed to play down production forecasts in order to create a more producer friendly atmosphere.

For a number of reasons production in Africa has tended to fall over the years but recent trends reducing government involvement have led to some improvement. Overnight miracles will not happen but a slight increase may be looked for in 1996/97.

Illegal cross border trade has made it difficult to assess production in Ethiopia in the past but measures have now been introduced to deal with that problem. It is expected that around 3.9 million bags will be produced this season which will keep the country at the top of the African producers' list. Uganda is expected to follow at 3.6 million bags though the problems across its borders could eventually affect output.

Third in Africa comes the Ivory Coast, which at one time was the leading African producer. Low returns led to crops being neglected for some years but a return of better prices has led the government to give financial inducements to growers. Around 3.8 million bags is the officially expected figure for 1996/97 but the long term target is to aim for a much higher output.

There was an astonishingly large crop in Mexico last season which resulted in an output in North and Central America of almost 19 million bags. This season the crop in Mexico is expected to fall slightly from 5.3 to 5.2 million bags. At just over 3.6 million bags the output in Guatemala will be largely unchanged from 1995/96.

Rains caused by Hurricane Marcos have ruined hopes for a higher crop in Honduras, where last year's production was 2.3 million bags. In Costa Rica the 1996/97 crop is forecast to fall to 2.3 million bags from 2.6 million bags last year due to damage from Hurricane Cesar. At 18.0 million bags output in the region is expected to drop by about 970,000 bags.

South America remains the dominant producing region and Brazil the leading producer. Output in 1996/97 in Brazil is forecast at 26 million bags, up by more than 10 million bags on the weather affected 1995/96 crop. Financial problems are affecting the industry in Colombia and output is expected to drop to 11.5 million bags, a fall of 1.4 million bags on the year. Total production in the region is put at 42.3 million bags, about 9 million bags up on the year.

Indonesia remains the largest producer in Asia and with a return from two years of drought we forecast the crop at 7.5 million bags, an increase of more than one million bags. Production in Vietnam continues to go from strength to strength. Good pre-harvest rains have boosted the 1996/97 crop's potential and we put it at 4.3 million bags, up from 4.1 million bags in 1995/96.

It is generally agreed that India will not reach its target of 4 million bags this year. It is a down year in the production cycle and weather conditions have not been too favourable. We are putting output at 3 million bags, a drop of 700,000 bags on the year.
Almost all Oceania's output is concentrated in Papua New Guinea. At 1.03 million bags we put output down by about 100,000 bags compared with last season.

The indications are that in 1996/97 producers will be able to continue their tight supply policy. Even if these production forecasts should be exceeded producers may hope that their retention scheme will prevent any sharp fall in prices.
